**No — being without teeth for years does not automatically rule out All-on-4.** Your jawbone does shrink after tooth loss, but All-on-4 was designed around that: two of the four implants are angled to reach the denser bone that remains, which often avoids bone grafting. A 3D scan at your free consultation shows exactly how much bone you have.

## What happens to your jawbone over time?

**When a tooth is gone, the bone under it slowly shrinks because it no longer gets pressure from chewing.** Most of the change happens early, and it continues more slowly for years.

<KeyStat value="29–63%" label="loss of ridge width in the first 6 to 7 months after an extraction" source="Tan et al., 2012" />

<KeyStat value="11–22%" label="loss of ridge height at 6 months after an extraction" source="Tan et al., 2012" />

## Why doesn't long-term tooth loss stop treatment?

**Because All-on-4 places implants where the bone is strongest.** Even people who lost their teeth 10 or 20 years ago can often get a new set. The two front implants go in straight; the two back implants are tilted to avoid areas where bone has thinned, such as near the sinuses in the upper jaw or the nerve in the lower jaw.

## How does the All-on-4 method work?

**Four implants support a full arch of fixed teeth.** In many cases, a temporary bridge is attached the same day. The final bridge is made after the implants have healed.

## Who may be a good candidate?

**People who have lost most or all of their teeth in one or both jaws, whose dentures move or affect daily life, or who want teeth that stay in.** Your health history, gum health, and bone volume all factor in, and only an in-person exam with a 3D scan can confirm candidacy.

## Why Renew for long-term denture wearers?

Many of our patients come to us after decades in dentures. Tom Szarski has been a denturist in Ottawa for over 20 years, and our implant surgeon, denturist, and lab work together under one roof, so your plan accounts for both the implants and the teeth that go on them.

Bone that has already shrunk is the subject of [dental implants with bone loss](/blog/dental-implants-with-bone-loss). Diabetes and smoking, as separate questions, are in [dental implants with diabetes or smoking](/blog/dental-implants-with-diabetes-or-smoking). A denture that clips on, rather than a fixed arch, is compared in [snap-on dentures versus All-on-4](/blog/snap-on-dentures-vs-all-on-4). Candidacy at the clinic starts on [what to expect](/what-to-expect).

## What did the original study actually time?

Maló, Rangert, and Nobre studied immediate function within two hours using four Brånemark implants to support fixed prostheses in completely edentulous mandibles. Forty-four patients received 176 immediately loaded implants and fixed complete-arch mandibular prostheses in acrylic. Five immediately loaded implants were lost before six months. Cumulative survival was 96.7 percent in the development group and 98.2 percent in the routine group. Prosthesis survival was 100 percent.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

Those rates belong to that retrospective mandibular series. They are not a description of the upper jaw, and they are not a script for the first weeks at home. This page does not copy the study's medication regimen into patient advice.

Same-day teeth, as a separate question, are discussed in [same-day dental implants](/blog/same-day-dental-implants-new-teeth-one-day). The clinic's visit sequence is on [what to expect](/what-to-expect).

## What should you not treat as a schedule?

The papers used here do not establish when swelling peaks, which foods are allowed on which day, or how many days of work you should book off. If a clinic gives you written aftercare, that sheet is the instruction for your case. This article will not invent a substitute.

Long-term complication rates from later follow-up, including mechanical problems years on, are not "the first weeks." How long the implants were still present in a later mandibular series is covered in [how long All-on-4 implants last](/blog/how-long-do-all-on-4-implants-last).

## Why call if it does not feel ordinary?

The 2017 World Workshop separates peri-implant health from disease. Health is the absence of redness, bleeding on probing, swelling, and suppuration. Peri-implantitis adds progressive bone loss, with bleeding or pus, deeper pockets or recession, and bone loss on a radiograph. Diagnosis needs a clinician.<Cite id="berglundh-2018" />

That is not a home test you can finish from soreness alone. If you already have an implant and it does not feel right, use [what to do next](/blog/dental-implant-not-feeling-right) and call [the clinic](/contact-us) at 613-841-6111. The quiz on this page is for people still choosing a treatment, not for someone who needs a clinician today.

## What did four-versus-six reviews actually find?

Sharaf, Wang, Mashrah, Xu, Haider, and He pooled 53 studies of maxillary fixed complete dentures: 20,251 implants in 4,713 arches, mean follow-up 3.8 years. Mean implant survival was 98.5% (95% CI 97.8 to 99.1) with four implants and 97% (95% CI 95.2 to 98.4) with six. That survival difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.06). Prosthesis survival was 99.8% versus 99.6% (p = 0.37). Mean marginal bone loss was 1.02 mm (95% CI 0.79 to 1.26) with four implants and 0.46 mm (95% CI 0.20 to 0.72) with six (p < 0.01).<Cite id="sharaf-2024" />

The abstract reports no significant difference in technical or mechanical complications, or in biological complications. The technical rates they calculated were 20.7 per 100 prostheses with four implants and 17.9 with six (p = 0.74). Biological rates were 2.0 and 0.8 (p = 0.20). A later conclusion sentence says six implants can decrease complications. That sentence is stronger than the tests. This page uses the tests.<Cite id="sharaf-2024" />

Shao and colleagues pooled 55 studies of the named All-on-4 and All-on-6 concepts. At one year, implant survival was 99.20% versus 100%. From one to five years it was 99.66% versus 98.55%. At five years or more it was 98.14% versus 97.50%. Short-term bone loss was 0.77 mm versus 0.85 mm. At five years it was 1.28 mm versus 0.94 mm. The authors report high long-term survival for both techniques and similar biological complications between them. They also note high heterogeneity, and only one randomized trial compared the two concepts directly.<Cite id="shao-2026" />

## Why is a pooled percentage not your implant count?

These are different papers. Sharaf is maxillary fixed dentures, and nearly every four-implant study in it used two straight implants and two tilted ones. Shao names All-on-4 and All-on-6 and still warns that most included studies were lower-level evidence. Putting 98.5% from one paper next to 98.14% from the other, as if they were one experiment, would invent a comparison neither group ran.<Cite id="sharaf-2024" /><Cite id="shao-2026" />

A longer mandibular series, with its own lost-to-follow-up problem, is in [how long All-on-4 implants lasted in that follow-up](/blog/how-long-do-all-on-4-implants-last). The original four-implant protocol is in [what All-on-4 meant in the 2003 series](/blog/what-is-all-on-4). Replacing teeth one by one is a different comparison, covered in [full arch treatment versus individual implants](/blog/full-arch-vs-individual-dental-implants).

## Why does Renew choose the number from the scan?

The [upper jaw implant](/services/upper-jaw-implants) page says some people are candidates for All-on-4 and others may benefit from six or more implants, depending on bone density and anatomy. A snap-on overdenture remains a removable option on that page.<Cite id="renew-upper" /> The treatment hub is [All-on-4 dental implants](/services/all-on-4-dental-implants). People comparing a whole arch with separate crowns can also read [full arch dental implants](/services/full-arch-dental-implants).

The implant surgeon places the implants. Tom Szarski, DD, is the denturist who designs and fits the teeth with the on-site lab. The free consultation includes a 3D scan. The number of implants is part of that plan. It is not copied out of a pooled percentage.

## What do published disease signs include?

Berglundh, Armitage, and the 2017 World Workshop define peri-implant health as the absence of erythema, bleeding on probing, swelling, and suppuration. Peri-implant mucositis is bleeding on gentle probing. Erythema, swelling, and suppuration may be there. They name plaque as the cause. Peri-implantitis is plaque-associated inflammation of the mucosa together with progressive loss of supporting bone. The clinical signs they list are bleeding on probing and/or suppuration, increased probing depths and/or recession, plus radiographic bone loss.<Cite id="berglundh-2018" />

That list is not a photograph you can take in a bathroom mirror. Probing depths and radiographs are clinic measurements.

## Is soreness after surgery the same list?

No. The workshop definitions are for peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis, not for the first days after an operation. This page does not turn a tight feeling, a bruise, or a tender gum into a failed implant. It also does not say a loose feeling proves failure. If the timing is the early weeks after All-on-4, read [what the studies do and do not time](/blog/all-on-4-recovery-first-weeks), and still call if you are worried. Longer follow-up, which is not the same question as this week's soreness, is in [how long All-on-4 implants last](/blog/how-long-do-all-on-4-implants-last).

## What does a bridge ask of the neighbouring teeth?

Hebel, Gajjar, and Hofstede published a peer-reviewed comparison in the Journal of the Canadian Dental Association in 2000, volume 66, pages 435 to 438. The options they discuss for a single tooth are a fixed partial denture, a resin-bonded restoration, and a single-tooth implant. They wrote that a conventional three-unit bridge is familiar work for most restorative dentists, and that it requires reduction of the abutment teeth. That reduction, they wrote, results in an increased incidence of endodontic therapy and root decay.<Cite id="hebel-2000" />

They drew a line at the condition of those teeth. Large existing restorations might make abutment preparation useful. Virgin teeth, or teeth with small restorations, would be damaged and placed at higher risk. They also wrote that cement loss or washout under a retainer can lead to tooth loss, and that a bridge is one restoration: if one part fails, the whole restoration fails, often with loss of an abutment tooth. The implant's advantage, in their words, is that the adjacent teeth stay in their current state of health and are not splinted into a larger restoration.<Cite id="hebel-2000" />

The paper says patients should hear both sides before choosing. It does not rank the options for a person who is losing many teeth at once.

## When is a full arch a different comparison?

A three-unit bridge borrows strength from two teeth to fill one space. When those neighbours are themselves failing, the 2000 article's premise (sound or restorable abutments beside a single gap) no longer describes the mouth. [Full arch treatment versus replacing teeth one by one](/blog/full-arch-vs-individual-dental-implants) is the comparison for a whole row of implant crowns versus one bridge on several implants. [Dentures compared with dental implants](/blog/dentures-vs-dental-implants) is the comparison for a removable plate. A clip-in denture versus a fixed All-on-4 bridge is in [snap-on dentures versus All-on-4](/blog/snap-on-dentures-vs-all-on-4).

[Full arch dental implants](/services/full-arch-dental-implants) is the service page for a fixed row. This article stays with the single-tooth evidence and points to those pages when the gap is no longer single.

## Why is a three-unit bridge a different job from a full jaw?

The journal article is explicit about its subject: replacement of a single tooth. Using it to argue for or against All-on-4 would stretch a three-unit bridge into a jaw it never measured.<Cite id="hebel-2000" /> The useful part, for someone with one or two failing teeth next to sound ones, is the preparation of those neighbours. The useful part, for someone whose remaining teeth are the problem, is noticing that the article does not cover that mouth.

The implant surgeon places implants. Tom Szarski, DD, is the denturist who designs and fits implant teeth and dentures with the on-site lab. A free consultation includes a 3D scan. The scan is what shows whether the neighbours can carry a bridge, or whether the plan has to be a denture or a full arch.

## How much bone changes after teeth are lost?

The bone that held a tooth loses the load of chewing. Tan, Wong, Wong, and Lang reviewed human studies that re-entered extraction sites. They reported horizontal bone loss of 29 to 63 percent and vertical bone loss of 11 to 22 percent after six months, with rapid reductions in the first three to six months. Horizontal percentage loss was about 32 percent at three months.<Cite id="tan-2012" />

Those are study means. They are not a measurement of your jaw. People who have been without teeth for years are the subject of [All-on-4 after years of missing teeth](/blog/all-on-4-dental-implants-after-years-of-missing-teeth). Diabetes and smoking, which are separate from bone volume, are in [dental implants with diabetes or smoking](/blog/dental-implants-with-diabetes-or-smoking).

## What was All-on-4 designed to do in a thin jaw?

Soto-Peñaloza and colleagues describe the concept as a way to maximize remnant bone in atrophic jaws, to provide immediate function, and to avoid regenerative procedures. The protocol they summarize places four implants in the anterior jaw, two axial and two angled posteriorly, to shorten the cantilever, supporting up to 12 teeth on a provisional fixed prosthesis that is loaded immediately.<Cite id="soto-2017" />

Their conclusion calls it a predictable approach for patients who do not prefer regenerative procedures. The same paper says the evidence is limited by sample size, follow-up, and patients lost along the way. This page does not repeat a survival percentage from that review, because the authors warn that the numbers can mislead.

The [All-on-4 service page](/services/all-on-4-dental-implants) is the clinic hub for that treatment. Candidacy for your mouth is discussed against [what to expect](/what-to-expect) at a consultation, after a 3D scan.

## What do the pooled smoking numbers say?

Chrcanovic, Albrektsson, and Wennerberg included 107 studies. Implants in smokers failed more often: risk ratio 2.23 (95% CI 1.96 to 2.53). Postoperative infection, in the studies that reported it, had a risk ratio of 2.01 (95% CI 1.09 to 3.72). They also found more marginal bone loss, mean difference 0.32 mm, but that analysis was highly heterogeneous (I² 95%), so this page does not treat 0.32 mm as a stable number. The authors say the results should be interpreted with caution because of uncontrolled confounding.<Cite id="chrcanovic-2015" />

## What did the diabetes review measure?

Al Ansari, Shahwan, and Chrcanovic included 89 publications: 5,510 implants in people with diabetes and 62,780 in people without. The odds ratio for failure was 1.777 (p < 0.001). The authors' conclusion calls that a 77.7% higher risk. Failures were more likely in type 1 than type 2 diabetes (odds ratio 4.477, p = 0.032). The failure difference was statistically significant in the maxilla and not in the mandible. Mean marginal bone loss differed by 0.776 mm (p = 0.027); that bone-loss analysis was also highly heterogeneous, so it is a pooled difference, not a measurement of your jaw.<Cite id="alansari-2022" />

## What did the McGill statement say about adhesive?

On 24 and 25 May 2002, a symposium at McGill University produced a consensus led by Feine, Carlsson, and colleagues, published in Gerodontology. Conventional dentures, they wrote, rely on the residual alveolar ridge and the mucosa for support and retention. Many people have trouble adapting, especially to the mandibular prosthesis. The sentence on adhesive is specific: "The widespread use of denture adhesives is one indication that these prostheses are inadequate for many denture wearers."<Cite id="feine-2002" />

They also wrote that numerous denture wearers report they cannot eat many foods, including hard or tough ones, and that diets change in unhealthy ways. That is a population statement. It does not measure one person's tube of adhesive, and this page will not turn it into a nutrition prescription.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

How a full denture compares with implants more broadly is in [dentures compared with dental implants](/blog/dentures-vs-dental-implants).

## Is an implant-held denture the same as All-on-4?

The implant denture in the McGill statement is a removable lower overdenture on two implants. All-on-4 is a fixed bridge on four implants. The trials behind the consensus compared mandibular two-implant overdentures with new conventional dentures, for 6 months to 9 years. Attachment type did not change the direction of the result: bar, ball, or magnet. Participants were significantly more satisfied. They found the overdenture more stable, rated chewing various foods as easier, and were more comfortable and spoke more easily. Quality-of-life ratings were higher for people who received the two-implant overdenture against a conventional upper denture than for people with new conventional dentures.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

The conclusion is just as specific. A conventional denture was no longer the most appropriate first choice for the edentulous mandible. A two-implant overdenture should become the first choice. The upper denture is the one they said people usually manage. The lower denture is the one that moves.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

That overdenture is the family of treatment described in [snap-on dentures versus All-on-4](/blog/snap-on-dentures-vs-all-on-4). It comes out. All-on-4 does not. The lower-jaw version of this evidence is in [a lower denture versus lower implants](/blog/lower-denture-vs-implants).

## Why does Renew separate adhesive, snap-on, and fixed teeth?

Adhesive is something a person adds to a denture that is already made. A snap-on denture is a denture retained by implants. A fixed bridge is screwed or attached so it stays in. The consensus is evidence for the middle option on a lower jaw, not a ranking of all three for every mouth.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

The implant surgeon places the implants. Tom Szarski, DD, is the denturist who designs and fits the teeth and the dentures with the on-site lab. A free consultation includes a 3D scan. ## Why do people look beyond dentures?

**Because dentures can move.** Some people have trouble chewing certain foods because their dentures shift in the mouth. Others worry about them lifting while speaking or laughing. And because a denture rests on the gums, the bone underneath keeps shrinking, so dentures tend to loosen over time and need relines.

## What makes dental implants different?

**An implant is a titanium post placed in the jawbone that acts like a tooth root.** Replacement teeth attach to the implants, so they don't rely on suction or adhesive. Because chewing forces reach the bone through the implants, they also help preserve the jawbone that dentures can't. What years without teeth do to that bone is in [dental implants with bone loss](/blog/dental-implants-with-bone-loss).

## Are dental implants comfortable?

**Once the mouth has healed, most patients say implants look and feel like natural teeth.** Because they are fixed in place, they don't rub or slip while eating or talking. Some soreness or swelling right after surgery is normal and usually settles within days.

**No.** There are several options, and the right one depends on your oral health, bone support, lifestyle, and budget. A dental professional checks all of these before recommending implants, which is why we start with a free consultation and a 3D scan.

## How do you care for dental implants?

**Brush, clean around the implants, and keep your regular check-ups.** Implants can last a long time with good home care. Your team will show you how to clean under a fixed bridge or around snap-on attachments.

Section 3 of the Denturism Act, 1991, says the practice of denturism is the assessment of arches missing some or all teeth, and the design, construction, repair, alteration, ordering, and fitting of removable dentures. ## What are individual dental implants?

**An individual implant replaces a single missing tooth.** A titanium post is placed in the jawbone, and after it heals, a custom crown is attached. Each missing tooth gets its own implant and crown.

## What are full arch dental implants?

**A full arch replaces most or all of the teeth in one jaw with a single bridge.** Several implants support the bridge, so you don't need one implant per tooth.

## How do they differ in practice?

**It comes down to how many teeth need replacing.** Replacing an entire row tooth by tooth would mean many implants and more surgery. A full arch spreads the bite across a few strategically placed implants, which is how All-on-4 restores a whole arch on four.

**Your consultation answers that with a 3D scan.** The number and location of missing teeth, the health of the teeth that remain, and your bone volume all shape the plan. You'll leave with a clear recommendation and one all-inclusive price.

## What did 10 to 18 years of follow-up show?

Maló, de Araújo Nobre, Lopes, Ferro, and Botto reported on 471 patients (286 women and 185 men, mean age 57.7 years), 1,884 implants, and 471 fixed full-arch mandibular prostheses placed with immediate function. Follow-up was 10 to 18 years. Twenty-seven patients had died (5.7%). One hundred forty-nine (31.6%) were lost to follow-up. Cumulative prosthetic survival was 98.8%. Implant cumulative survival was 93% and success was 91.7% up to 18 years.<Cite id="malo-2019" />

Previous biological complications had a hazard ratio of 4.43 for implant failure. Biological complications were 11.8% at implant level. Mechanical complications were 36.7%. For marginal bone loss greater than 3 mm, the odds ratios they reported included smoking 2.72, previous failure of a contiguous implant 3.89, and a biological complication 8.11.<Cite id="malo-2019" />

A systematic review of the All-on-4 concept found mean cumulative implant survival of 94% to 98% between 72 and 132 months, and prosthesis survival of 99% to 100% at 12 months. The authors did not find a significant difference between axial and tilted implants or between maxilla and mandible. The major prosthetic complication they name is fracture of an acrylic prosthesis. They ask for larger randomized trials with long follow-up.<Cite id="gaonkar-2021" />

## Why one clinic's series is not your forecast?

The 93% figure is a cumulative survival estimate from one group's lower-jaw patients, after dropping a large share of people from later visits. It does not tell you how long your bridge will last. It does not include a price, and it is not a personal success rate.

People comparing the idea of All-on-4 with staying in dentures can read [why people choose All-on-4](/blog/why-people-are-choosing-all-on-4). The treatment hub is [All-on-4 dental implants](/services/all-on-4-dental-implants).

## What does maintenance change?

The Maló series linked biological complications with later failure, and linked smoking and prior implant trouble with more bone loss.<Cite id="malo-2019" /> This page will not turn those associations into a rule for your chart. Smoking and diabetes, as separate pooled analyses, are in [dental implants with diabetes or smoking](/blog/dental-implants-with-diabetes-or-smoking).

## Why do people struggle with a lower denture?

The McGill consensus statement, from a May 2002 symposium and published by Feine, Carlsson, and colleagues, puts the problem in one sentence. Complete denture wearers are usually able to wear an upper denture without problems, but many struggle to eat with the complete lower denture because it is too mobile. Conventional dentures rely on the residual alveolar ridge and the mucosa for support and retention. Many patients have trouble adapting, especially to the mandibular prosthesis.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

The widespread use of denture adhesive is one indication, they wrote, that these prostheses are inadequate for many wearers. That line is unpacked in [denture adhesive versus implants](/blog/denture-adhesive-vs-implants). The foods they mention are hard or tough ones that wearers report being unable to eat. This page does not add a calorie claim on top of that sentence.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

[Dentures compared with dental implants](/blog/dentures-vs-dental-implants) is the broader comparison. The upper plate, which the statement treats as the manageable one, is in [an upper denture versus upper All-on-4](/blog/upper-denture-vs-all-on-4).

## Is the recommended implant denture the same as All-on-4?

The recommended implant denture is a removable overdenture on two lower implants, and All-on-4 is a fixed bridge on four. Mandibular two-implant overdentures were superior to conventional dentures in randomized and non-randomized trials lasting from six months to nine years. Whatever the attachment (bar, ball, or magnet), people were significantly more satisfied than with new conventional dentures. They found the implant overdenture more stable, rated chewing as easier, and were more comfortable and spoke more easily. Quality of life was significantly higher for patients who received the two-implant overdenture opposing a complete maxillary denture.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

The conclusion follows that evidence: restoration of the edentulous mandible with a conventional denture is no longer the most appropriate first choice, and a two-implant overdenture should become the first choice. Two implants. A denture that is still a denture. [Snap-on dentures versus All-on-4](/blog/snap-on-dentures-vs-all-on-4) is where the fixed four-implant bridge is set beside that clip-in denture.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

## Why does Renew still offer more than one lower option?

The consensus sets a minimum they wanted recognized: two implants and an overdenture, rather than a conventional lower denture alone.<Cite id="feine-2002" /> A fixed lower bridge uses more implants and does not come out. The [lower jaw implants](/services/lower-jaw-implants) page is the clinic's page for that jaw. Which of those prostheses fits depends on the bone, the opposing teeth, and whether the person wants a denture they remove.

The implant surgeon places the implants. Tom Szarski, DD, is the denturist who designs and fits the overdenture or the fixed teeth with the on-site lab. A free consultation includes a 3D scan. The [meet the team](/meet-your-dentist) page says Renew's sister clinic, Orléans Denture Clinic, operates a full on-site lab staffed by registered dental technicians. ## What do the studies say the lab is building?

Maló, Rangert, and Nobre describe the object, not the postal address of the laboratory. The same-day bridge was acrylic, reinforced with a metal strip, with at least 10 teeth. For the development group, the later prosthesis was cast metal in the first seven patients and a milled titanium Procera bridge in the other 23, made 4 to 6 months after surgery. Nine early acrylic bridges fractured and were repaired; after the acrylic was thickened, the routine group had no fractures in the reported follow-up.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

That is evidence about materials and timing. It is not evidence that a lab inside the clinic building produces higher implant survival than a lab down the street. [What All-on-4 meant in that protocol](/blog/what-is-all-on-4) keeps the surgical definition separate from the workshop.

## How do same-day implants work?

**The implants and a temporary set of teeth are placed in one visit.** Traditionally, an implant is placed, the jaw heals around it for a few months, and then teeth are attached. With same-day implants, the temporary teeth go on right away, so you have a complete smile while the bone heals. The final bridge replaces the temporary once healing is complete.

## Who may qualify for same-day teeth?

**People with enough stable jawbone and healthy gums have the best chance.** The implants must be firm on the day of surgery to carry a temporary bridge. Your surgeon checks your jawbone, gums, and overall oral health with a 3D scan before recommending it.

## Why do people prefer same-day treatment?

**Leaving with teeth the same day saves time and removes the stress of going without.** Patients tell us it also helps them feel confident at work and with family during the healing months.

## What should you expect after the visit?

**Some soreness, swelling, or mild pain for a few days is normal.** Soft foods make the first weeks more comfortable while the implants bond with the bone. Your team schedules follow-ups to check healing and adjust the temporary teeth.

## When are one-day teeth not the right option?

**When the bone is too thin, gum disease is active, or other treatment is needed first.** In those cases a staged plan is safer, and it still ends with fixed teeth. The goal is the right result for the long term, not the fastest one.

## Why Renew for same-day implants?

Same-day teeth depend on the lab. At Renew, the lab is in the same building, with a PM7 milling machine, Asiga digital printers, and 3Shape scanners, so your temporary bridge can be designed and made while you're here. Sedation is available if you'd rather sleep through the procedure.

## Which levels does Ontario define?

The College's authorization page separates minimal sedation (nitrous oxide and oxygen, or a single oral sedative), oral moderate sedation, parenteral moderate sedation, deep sedation, and general anaesthesia. Parenteral routes listed there include intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, submucosal, and intranasal. Deep sedation means the person is not easily aroused and responds to repeated or painful stimulation. General anaesthesia means the person is not arousable even by painful stimulation.<Cite id="rcdso-levels" />

Dentists need current authorization to administer any level, including minimal. Facilities that provide oral moderate sedation, parenteral sedation, deep sedation, or general anaesthesia need a facility permit. A facility that provides only minimal sedation (nitrous oxide-oxygen or oral minimal) does not require a facility permit. A physician who gives sedation or anaesthesia in a dental office must register with the College and stay registered with the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.<Cite id="rcdso-overview" />

## What does this clinic publish?

Renew's sedation page describes three options in its own words: an oral medication taken before the visit, IV sedation administered by a trained sedation professional, and general anaesthesia for people who want to be completely asleep, with a qualified anaesthesia team. The same page says you will need someone to drive you home.<Cite id="renew-sedation" />

That is the clinic's published description. It is not, by itself, a copy of the facility permit. At the consultation, ask which authorization covers the visit you are booking. The public register is the College's record. This article does not state which permit the clinic holds.

## Which one comes out at night?

Renew's denture-alternative page says a snap-on denture, also called an overdenture, clips onto connectors on two or four implants. You can take it out to clean it. During the day it is meant to stay locked.<Cite id="renew-snapon" /> That is the practical difference people feel: it is still a denture.

The same clinic's All-on-4 page describes a full set of upper or lower teeth fixed to four implants in the jaw, and says these teeth stay in, unlike removable dentures.<Cite id="renew-allon4" /> A fixed bridge is cleaned in the mouth. It is not dropped into a cup at night.

The wider comparison, including conventional dentures, is in [dentures versus dental implants](/blog/dentures-vs-dental-implants).

## What does the published All-on-4 concept specify?

Soto-Peñaloza and colleagues describe four implants in the anterior jaw, two of them axial and two angled, supporting a provisional fixed prosthesis that is loaded immediately, with up to 12 teeth. They say the concept was developed for atrophic jaws and to avoid regenerative procedures. They also say the evidence is limited.<Cite id="soto-2017" />

That paper is about a fixed prosthesis. It is not a description of a denture that snaps on and off. If you are weighing the fixed version after years without teeth, the candidacy article is [All-on-4 after years of missing teeth](/blog/all-on-4-dental-implants-after-years-of-missing-teeth).

## Why the fixed option is a different job?

Ontario's Denturism Act defines denturism as the assessment of arches missing some or all teeth, and the design, construction, repair, alteration, ordering, and fitting of removable dentures. Fitting and dispensing in the Act are also about removable dentures.<Cite id="denturism-act" /> A fixed All-on-4 bridge is not that appliance.

## What were the first teeth in the original series?

Maló, Rangert, and Nobre delivered an acrylic prosthesis, reinforced by a metal strip, within two hours after the four lower implants were placed. It was designed to hold a minimum of 10 teeth, because the tilted back implants moved the screw holes forward, usually to about the second premolar. Prosthesis survival in the series was 100%.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

Patzelt, Bahat, Reynolds, and Strub reviewed 13 papers and 4,804 implants, of which 74 failed, 74% of those failures inside the first 12 months. They counted 1,201 prostheses incorporated within 48 hours. Mean cumulative survival at 36 months was 99.0% for implants (standard deviation 1.0) and 99.9% for prostheses (standard deviation 0.3). Mean bone loss was 1.3 mm (standard deviation 0.4). They found no significant difference between upper and lower jaws, or between straight and tilted implants. They also wrote that the evidence was limited, that studies of five years or more were scarce, and that randomized trials were needed. The complication they single out is fracture of the all-acrylic bridge.<Cite id="patzelt-2014" />

The day-one visit itself, including what "same day" does and does not include, is in [same-day implants and new teeth in one day](/blog/same-day-dental-implants-new-teeth-one-day). The sore-mouth weeks that follow are in [the first weeks after All-on-4](/blog/all-on-4-recovery-first-weeks).

## Why did some of those acrylic teeth fracture?

Nine acrylic prostheses in the development group, 30%, had repairable fractures. Screw fracture or loosening sometimes came with those breaks. The routine-group bridges were then made with more material thickness, and the acrylic was cured under higher pressure. That group had no fractures in the reported follow-up. The authors wrote that a reinforced acrylic prosthesis might be used as a lower-cost final in that protocol. They also built metal or milled titanium finals for the development group, which is a different object from the two-hour acrylic.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

A fracture of the plastic teeth in that series did not, by itself, mean the bridge was lost. The implants were scored on their own life table. When one immediately loaded implant failed, the provisional survived on the other three.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

People leave with teeth on day one. Feine, Carlsson, and the McGill panel wrote this in 2002: "Complete denture wearers are usually able to wear an upper denture without problems, but many struggle to eat with the complete lower denture because it is too mobile." The studies they cite found higher quality-of-life ratings when people received a two-implant lower overdenture opposing a conventional maxillary denture, compared with new conventional dentures. All-on-4, as a technique, is four implants and a fixed bridge. It can be planned on an upper jaw. It does not come out, and it does not sit as a plate on the ridge the way a complete denture does. The McGill statement never compared that fixed upper bridge with an upper denture. Treating the consensus as an upper-jaw verdict would reverse the jaw they actually studied.<Cite id="feine-2002" />

[What All-on-4 meant in the original lower-jaw series](/blog/what-is-all-on-4) is the definition. [Snap-on dentures versus All-on-4](/blog/snap-on-dentures-vs-all-on-4) separates a clip-in denture from a fixed bridge. Maló, Rangert, and Nobre published a retrospective series of immediately loaded complete-arch prostheses in edentulous mandibles, or mandibles with hopeless teeth. Those extra implants were not part of the provisional bridge. The authors later decided they were not needed. The last third of the patients received only the four immediately loaded implants. When an immediately loaded implant was lost, the provisional bridge survived on the remaining three until a replacement was added.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

Life tables show four immediately loaded implants lost before six months in the development group and one in the routine group. Cumulative implant survival was 96.7% and 98.2%. Prosthesis survival was 100%.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

## Is All-on-4 the same thing as any full arch?

A full arch means a bridge that replaces a whole row. All-on-4 is one way to support that row: four implants, with the back ones tilted, loaded early. [How four implants compared with six in later reviews](/blog/all-on-4-vs-all-on-6) is a separate question, and the reviews do not treat the count as interchangeable for every jaw. ## When did the original series make a final prosthesis?

Maló, Rangert, and Nobre split the 44 lower jaws. For the development group, final prostheses were made 4 to 6 months after surgery. The first seven patients had conventional cast-metal frameworks. The other 23 had milled titanium Procera implant bridges. Those finals incorporated the rescue implants that had been left out of the provisional. The paper's figure caption also describes a final prosthesis made within 6 months using the Procera implant bridge.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

The routine group is the important limit. Those patients kept the provisional acrylic for the follow-up the authors reported, aside from two who received titanium frameworks after 12 months. The authors also wrote that a reinforced acrylic bridge might serve as a final in that protocol. Reporting only "4 to 6 months" would hide that second path.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

What the two-hour acrylic was, and why nine of the early ones fractured, is in [temporary teeth after All-on-4](/blog/temporary-teeth-after-all-on-4). The surgery-day visit is in [same-day implants and new teeth in one day](/blog/same-day-dental-implants-new-teeth-one-day).

## Why is there no single month on this page?

The 4-to-6-month interval belongs to 30 people in one mandibular series, and it was the interval before a metal or titanium framework. It was not the interval for the routine group. Healing, the opposing teeth, a repair, or a lost implant changed individual stories inside that same paper: some replacement implants were loaded when the final was placed, around 4 or 5 months in the cases they describe.<Cite id="malo-2003" />

A webpage that offered one month would be inventing a protocol the study did not use for everyone. The first weeks of eating and soreness are a different timeline, in [the first weeks after All-on-4](/blog/all-on-4-recovery-first-weeks).
